title: Homeless by Choice
dek: A tongue-in-cheek ledger: the guy in the doorway versus the guy paying rent. We ran the real numbers. Somebody's getting ripped off.
body: Every Seattle office worker has had the thought. You're on the 7 at 7:40 a.m., your ORCA card just ate another three bucks, your rent went up, and you watch a guy stretch out in a doorway on Third without a care in the world. And a little voice says: what if he's the smart one?
So the Sinner did what nobody at City Hall has time to do. We ran the numbers. Real ones, with receipts. Grab your $4.50 coffee and follow along.
## Option A: Homeless by choice
Let's be generous and assume our hero qualifies for everything Washington offers. Here's the monthly haul.
= Basic Food (SNAP), max for one | $306
= Aged, Blind or Disabled cash grant | $450
= Lifeline phone discount | $9.25
= ORCA LIFT pass savings ($36 vs. $108) | $72
= Hot meals on the waterfront, Mon–Sat | Free
= Food bank groceries, toiletries, clothes | Free
= A spot at Tent City 3 (resident-run camp) | Free
= Apple Health (Medicaid): doctor, prescriptions | $0 premium, $0 copays
= Cash and benefits in hand, best case | ~$837
= What the state spends on his health care | ~$499
= The full package | ~$1,336 | tot

Not bad for doing nothing, right? Rent: zero. Utilities: zero. Student loans: who's going to find you? Groceries come from one of the roughly 30 neighborhood food banks in the Seattle Food Committee network, and some of them hand out clothes and diapers too, while spots like Nielsen's Pastries in Lower Queen Anne keep a free cupboard of clothes and hygiene supplies. A bed? Tent City 3, the resident-run camp organized with SHARE/WHEEL, takes about 100 people, with a kitchen tent, a warming tent with a TV, and city-paid portable toilets. And the doctor is on the house: Washington's Apple Health has no premiums, no copays and no deductibles, prescriptions included. The state spent about $5,993 per expansion adult in 2024, roughly $499 a month, according to KFF. Our office worker pays $120 a month for his share of insurance and still gets a copay every time he sees a doctor.

Now the fine print, which the brochure leaves out. That $450 cash grant only goes to people who are 65 or older, blind, or too sick or disabled to work for at least a year. So to win the jackpot, first get old, blind or seriously ill. Congratulations.

The rest of the fine print: Tent City 3 runs on a code of conduct that requires sobriety, nonviolence and pitching in, and it fills up. When it was at capacity this year, demand outran the spots. The food banks are free, but you're carrying it all back to a tent.
## Option B: The office worker

Meet our control subject: a Seattle-area office and admin worker making the local average of $30.27 an hour. That's about $62,962 a year, or roughly $4,367 a month after federal taxes. Washington, bless it, doesn't take an income tax. It just takes everything else.
= Median 1-bedroom rent (Apartment List, Oct 2026) | $1,948
= Student loan, average payment | $434
= Groceries for one (USDA) | $356
= Health insurance, employee share | $120
= ORCA monthly pass | $108
= Coffee habit at $4.50 a cup | $94.50
= Internet | $84.87
= Phone | $76
= Electricity, City Light | $65
= Renter's insurance | $18
= Monthly cost of being a responsible adult | ~$3,304 | tot

Subtract that from take-home pay and our office worker clears about $1,063 a month. Before parking, before a night out at the Crocodile, before the transmission dies. Do the math and the spreadsheet says the guy in the doorway is up $837 in cash and benefits, about $1,336 once you count the health care the state picks up, while you're up $1,063 after working 160 hours. On paper, he's out-earning you without clocking in. Case closed?
## The part of the spreadsheet nobody reads
Not quite. The ledger has a few more lines, and they don't round in his favor.

There are 18,365 people homeless in King County, according to this year's count, up 9 percent from 2024. Sixty-four percent of them are outside, not in shelter. The county has roughly one shelter bed for every three homeless people, and it lost 689 beds this year. So the 'free bed' costs the city about $28,000 a year to run, and there's a two-out-of-three chance you won't get one.

Since 2022, the city's Unified Care Team has done more than 5,000 encampment and vehicle removals. During one stretch of 2023, only 11 percent of shelter offers made during sweeps led to a placement. Translation: your 'free housing' is a tent that gets thrown in a dump truck every few months.

And the big one. The median age at death for homeless people examined by the King County Medical Examiner was 51. For everyone else, 62. Eleven years. That's the real price tag, and no benefits program covers it.
> Rent: $1,948. Dying eleven years early: priceless.
## The Sinner's verdict

Homeless by choice is a great bar joke and a terrible life plan. The punchline isn't that the guy in the doorway is living large. It's that a full-time worker in this city can do everything right and still end the month with about a thousand bucks between him and the doorway.

Meanwhile the regional homelessness authority has spent nearly $1.1 billion over five years while the count went up, and its budget hole just grew to $16.7 million. Seattle and King County plan to take back their contracts in January 2027.

So the next time you feel jealous on the 7, remember: you're not paying rent to a landlord. You're paying to stay alive eleven years longer. Tip your barista. And maybe vote like the doorway is a lot closer than you think.
